title: While and then
intro: This unit is about linking events, the way you do when you tell a story. `-(y)ken` sets one situation as the background of another: *Eve giderken ekmek aldım* (On my way home I bought bread). `-(y)Ip` joins two actions of the same person in the same tense: *Eve gidip yattım* (I went home and went to bed). And a few words put events in order or give reasons: *önce, sonra, ondan sonra, en sonunda, çünkü, bu yüzden, yine de*.

blocks.text: `-(y)ken` means **while** or **when** something is the case. It goes on a noun or an adjective, on a locative, or on a verb in the aorist. Like the `-ki` of [unit 10](gp-ki-adjective), it never changes: no harmony, no t for d, always *-ken*. After a vowel, it takes the buffer y of [A1 unit 3](gp-buffer-letters).

**No person, no tense.** *Çocukken* serves for every person and every time: the main verb gives both. The subject is usually the same in both parts: *Çocukken çok yaramazdım* (When I was a child, I was very naughty). With a different subject, say who: *Ben çocukken burada bir park vardı* (When I was a child, there was a park here).

**On verbs**, `-ken` goes after the aorist of [unit 4](gp-aorist-forms), whose vowel you already know: *gider* → *giderken* (while going, on the way), *gelir* → *gelirken*, *okur* → *okurken*, *yer* → *yerken*. It says what is going on when something else happens, or where you are on the way: *Eve giderken* (on the way home), *Gelirken ekmek al* (Buy some bread on your way here).

blocks.text: The main verb can be in any tense or mood: *Tatildeyken seni arayacağım* (I'll call you while I'm on holiday), *Ders çalışırken müzik dinlerim* (I listen to music while I study), *Yemek yerken konuşma!* (Don't talk while you eat!). With two different people, `-ken` can also set them against each other: *Herkes çalışırken sen uyuyorsun!* (Everyone is working while you sleep!)
**Iken.** The suffix comes from a word, *iken*, which formal writing still uses separately, with no buffer: *çocuk iken*, *evde iken*, *hasta iken*. Speech always uses the suffix.

items.en: When I was a child, I was very naughty.
When I was a student, this café didn't exist.
When I'm at home, I always listen to music.
On my way home, I dropped by the supermarket.
Could you buy some bread on your way here?
Don't talk on the phone while you're driving.

blocks.text: On a verb, `-ken` needs the aorist: *giderken*, *okurken*, never *gitken* or *okuken*. And it never harmonizes: *okurken*, *çocukken*, not *okurkan*.
The tense goes on the main verb, never on `-ken`: *Çocukken mutluydum* (I was happy as a child), not *Çocuktukken*.
After the `-mIş` of [unit 2](gp-mis-intro), `-ken` means **since … anyway, while you're at it**: *Gelmişken bir çay iç* (Since you're here, have a tea).
English needs several words for `-ken`: **while**, **when**, **as a child**, **on the way**. French often uses en + participle: en rentrant, *eve dönerken*.

When one person does two things one after the other, Turkish usually puts the first verb in `-(y)Ip` and gives tense and person only to the last: *Markete gidip ekmek aldım* (I went to the shop and bought bread). `-Ip` follows four-way harmony (*-ıp, -ip, -up, -üp*), takes the buffer y after a vowel (*okuyup*, *bekleyip*), and the t of *git-* and *et-* becomes d, as before any suffix that starts with a vowel: *gidip*, *yardım edip*.

blocks.label: -(y)Ip
lines: stem + -(y)Ip … last verb with tense and person

blocks.text: **The last verb decides.** Tense, mood and person all come from the final verb, and `-Ip` borrows them: *Oturup çay içtik* (We sat down and had tea), *Oturup çay içelim* (Let's sit down and have tea), *Eve gidip dinleneceğim* (I'll go home and rest), *Gidip bak!* (Go and have a look!), *Her sabah kalkıp koşarım* (Every morning I get up and run).
**The negative** `-mAyIp` negates only its own verb and often means **instead of**: *Okula gitmeyip evde kaldı* (She didn't go to school; she stayed at home).

**-Ip or ve?** *Markete gittim ve ekmek aldım* is correct, but sounds like a list of separate facts; `-Ip` ties the two actions into one event, and it is what people say. When the subjects differ, use *ve* or two clauses: *Ben yemek yaptım, Ali bulaşıkları yıkadı.*

items.en: I went to the shop and bought bread.
Let's sit down and talk a little.
I read the book and gave it back.
He got up and opened the window.
She didn't go to school; she stayed at home.

items.tr: Ali her gün Ankara'ya gidip geliyor.
items.seg: Ali her gün Ankara'ya gid|ip geliyor.
items.en: Ali commutes to Ankara every day.
items.note: *gidip gelmek*, to go and come back: a fixed pair

blocks.text: `-Ip` takes no tense and no person: *Gittip* or *gittimip* don't exist. Only the last verb carries them: *Gidip aldım*.
Both actions belong to one subject. *Ali gelip Ayşe gitti* is wrong; say *Ali geldi, Ayşe gitti*.
English **go and see**, **sit down and talk** are close to `-Ip`. Turkish uses it much more, for almost any chain of actions: *Kapıyı açıp çıktı* (She opened the door and went out).

sections.title: Önce, sonra, bu yüzden: telling a story

blocks.text: To put events in order, Turkish uses *önce* (first), *sonra* (then, later), *ondan sonra* (after that) and *en sonunda* (in the end, finally). To give a reason or a result: *çünkü* (because, [A1 unit 4](gp-question-words)) and *bu yüzden* (so, that's why). To say that something happened anyway: *yine de* (still, even so).

head: Word
Meaning
Example
English
rows: After that I went into a meeting.
In the end I went back home.
I'm tired because I got up early.
I got up early, so I'm tired.
I was tired; still, I went to the cinema.

blocks.text: **Önce and sonra** now have three uses each. After a time span: *iki gün önce* (two days ago, [unit 1](gp-time-past)), *iki gün sonra* (two days later). After the ablative: *yemekten önce*, *yemekten sonra* (before, after the meal, [unit 9](gp-postp-ablative)). Alone, at the start of a step: *Önce ellerini yıka, sonra sofraya otur* (First wash your hands, then sit down at the table). *Ondan sonra* is simply *sonra* after *o* in the ablative: **after that**.

**Çünkü or bu yüzden?** Both link a cause and its effect, in opposite orders. *Çünkü* comes before the cause: *Geç kaldım, çünkü otobüsü kaçırdım* (I was late because I missed the bus). *Bu yüzden* comes before the result: *Otobüsü kaçırdım, bu yüzden geç kaldım* (I missed the bus, so I was late). *O yüzden* and *bunun için* ([unit 9](gp-postp-nominative)) mean the same as *bu yüzden*.

**Yine de** admits a fact and goes against it, often after *ama*: *Hava soğuktu, ama yine de denize girdik* (It was cold, but we still went into the sea). *Yine* alone means **again**: *Yine geç kaldın!* (You're late again!)

items.tr: Önce duş aldım, sonra kahvaltı yaptım.
items.en: First I had a shower, then I had breakfast.
After that we went back home.

items.tr: Otobüsü kaçırdım, bu yüzden geç kaldım.
items.en: I missed the bus, so I was late.
I was late because I missed the bus.

items.tr: Çok yorgunduk, ama yine de dağa çıktık.
items.en: We were very tired, but we still climbed the mountain.
In the end the bus came.

lines.tr: Çünkü çok işim vardı. Önce bankaya gidip para çektim, sonra postaneye uğradım.
lines.en: Because I had a lot to do. First I went to the bank and took out money, then I dropped by the post office.

lines.tr: Eve dönerken yağmur yağdı, bu yüzden çok ıslandım. En sonunda eve gelip hemen yattım.
lines.en: On the way back home it rained, so I got very wet. In the end I came home and went straight to bed.

blocks.text: *Bu yüzden* means **so**, not **because**. *Hastaydım, bu yüzden gelmedim* is **I was ill, so I didn't come**.
*Sonunda* ([unit 2](a2-u02)) and *en sonunda* both mean **finally**; *en sonunda* stresses that it was the last step, often after a long wait.

summary: `-(y)ken` means **while, when**: on nouns and locatives (*çocukken*, *evdeyken*) and on the aorist (*giderken*, *okurken*). It never changes, and has no person or tense of its own.
On a verb, `-ken` follows the aorist: *giderken*, never *gitken*. Formal writing may use *iken* as a word.
`-(y)Ip` joins two actions of one subject; only the last verb carries tense and person: *Gidip aldım*, *Oturup konuşalım*.
`-Ip` harmonizes four ways and softens *git-* and *et-*: *alıp, gelip, oturup, görüp, gidip, okuyup*. The negative is `-mAyIp`: *gitmeyip*.
*Önce, sonra, ondan sonra, en sonunda* put events in order.
*Çünkü* introduces the cause; *bu yüzden* the result. *Yine de* means **still, even so**.
